expansion:
A is correct: the macula remains attached. The presentation is consistent with rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD): the lecture describes RRD as a detachment caused by a retinal tear or break, through which vitreous fluid enters the subretinal space, and lists high myopia as a common cause (L20, slide 6). It also identifies floaters, flashes, and a “curtain” or peripheral shadow as RRD symptoms (L20, slide 11). Preserved central acuity of 6/6 is explained by sparing of the macula; because the macula mediates central visual acuity, keeping it attached preserves central function and is the key favourable prognostic feature (not taken from the course material). The lecture itself does not teach macula-on versus macula-off detachment or prognostic timing, so this prognostic claim is not taken from the course material.

B is wrong. Younger age is not the principal reason for the favourable visual prognosis in this vignette. The relevant prognostic distinction is whether the macula is attached, rather than the patient’s age (not taken from the course material). Indeed, the lecture lists aging as a common cause of RRD, not as the favourable feature determining visual outcome here (L20, slide 6).

C is wrong. Presence of a natural crystalline lens is not the factor accounting for preserved central visual acuity in an established RRD. Lens status can affect retinal-detachment risk in some clinical settings, but it does not outweigh macular attachment as the determinant of central visual prognosis in this scenario (not taken from the course material).

D is wrong. Normal intraocular pressure does not explain the good visual prognosis. The retinal-detachment lecture does not cover intraocular-pressure findings in retinal detachment; the decisive feature is macular sparing (not taken from the course material).
objective: The fact tested is that a macula-on retinal detachment has a more favourable visual prognosis because central retinal function is preserved.
